items.headline: ‘I’m Really Terrified’: A Mathematician Grapples With AI’s Recent Breakthroughs
items.dek: Steven Strogatz coauthored a book about how math is moving beyond human understanding. He spoke with WIRED about the seismic impact artificial intelligence has had on his life’s work.
items.author: Isabella Ward
items.caption: WIRED headline, dek and puzzle illustration
items.notes: Article lede: "Steven Strogatz starts to cry when he talks about the artificial-intelligence-driven breakthroughs in his field over the past week."

items.dek: “I think the year 2026 is going to be remembered as either an annus mirabilis or annus horribilis for mathematics because so much has happened.” — Steven Strogatz
items.author: Isabella Ward
items.caption: Verbatim quote
items.notes: Also: “Instinctively, I'm really terrified.” And co-author Alex Townsend: “I feel totally threatened by it.”

items.headline: On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem
items.dek: We’re sharing a solution to the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the Millennium Prize Problems. This proof, produced by an internal OpenAI system, shows that the dynamics of the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid motion can develop a singularity in finite time.
items.caption: OpenAI announcement (text verified via page load; screenshot blocked by Cloudflare)
items.notes: Same page: "To solve the Navier–Stokes problem, we used an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra. We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models."

items.headline: FINITE TIME BLOWUP FOR NAVIER–STOKES
items.dek: Abstract. For every positive viscosity, we construct a solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations that starts from rest and develops unbounded velocity in finite time while maintaining uniformly bounded kinetic energy.
items.author: OPENAI
items.caption: Title page of the 166-page AI-produced proof (author line: "OPENAI"), rendered from the official PDF
Figure 1 of the proof: the swirling fluid core shrinking toward a finite-time singularity (t1<t2<t3)

items.headline: Navier-Stokes Announcement
items.dek: Today, CMI shares in the excitement of the global mathematical community as we contemplate the announcement that the Navier-Stokes problem has apparently been settled. We hope to see waves of new human understanding unleashed as the innovations behind this work are analysed and interrogated.
items.caption: Key paragraph from the Clay Institute statement
items.notes: Statement also: "The process is deliberately unhurried, but we will provide updates." Prize not awarded; OpenAI says it will not claim it.

items.dek: "Since August 28 we have been training a new internal model that has exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics..." Note that they are openly admitting they used training data from a period after we found our result. Is it ethical to use customer's data to try to scoop their customer?
items.author: Tristan Buckmaster (NYU)
items.caption: Buckmaster accuses OpenAI of using customer (Codex) data to scoop him

items.dek: the indiscriminate automated strip-mining of open problems for solutions may destroy the ecosystem from which the next generation of mathematical techniques, problems, and practitioners would have developed, similarly to how using excavators to dig out treasures from an archeological site destroys the rich historical context...
items.author: Terence Tao
items.caption: Tao (quoting Hugo Duminil-Copin) on AI strip-mining open problems
items.notes: Phrase originates with Duminil-Copin (proofsandprompts.com, Aug 30 2026), amplified by Tao. Fortune attributed it to Tao.

items.dek: An example occured just today, in which we were treated to the unedifying spectacle of no fewer than three separate AI companies race to announce their own improvement on the bounded gaps between prime result...
items.author: Terence Tao
items.caption: Tao on three AI companies racing on the prime-gaps problem

items.dek: A group of 25 Fields Medalists, including myself, have made a joint declaration on Math and AI
items.author: Terence Tao
items.caption: Tao announces the Fields Medalists' declaration (667 boosts)

items.dek: "We are not trying to meet some abstract production quota of definitions, theorems and proofs. The measure of our success is whether what we do enables people to understand and think more clearly and effectively about mathematics." — William Thurston (now the splash at the top of Tao's blog)
items.author: Terence Tao
items.caption: Aftermath: Tao's blog now carries a Thurston quote banner and a stream of AI-and-math guest posts
items.notes: Since Sep 7 the blog has run near-daily AI posts: "After Math" (Sep 12, De Toffoli & Duede guest post: "Not all answers are solutions."), Joint Statement about Mathathon (Sep 28), "Two reports" (AGMAI recommendations, Sep 30), "arXiv updates its rate limiting policy" (Oct 1), "What does the advent of powerful AI models mean for mathematicians like me?" (Oct 3). Note the Sep 12 "After Math" post is a guest post, not Tao's own words.

items.headline: After Math
items.dek: “Not all answers are solutions.” / “AI presents mathematics not with an ending but with a choice about what mathematical practice should become.”
items.outlet: What's new (Terence Tao's blog), guest post
items.author: Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede
items.caption: Guest post on Tao's blog; opens by quoting Buckmaster: “This is a Deep Blue–Kasparov moment.”

items.headline: A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics
items.dek: Over the last few months, the mathematical capabilities of LLMs have improved dramatically, to the point that they can solve major outstanding problems in many fields of mathematics. However, the push by AI companies to solve mathematical problems as a benchmark is detrimental to the science of mathematics, and to the mathematical community. The goals of the AI companies and the goals of the mathematical community are severely misaligned.
items.author: 25+ Fields Medalists incl. Terence Tao
items.caption: Declaration title + opening paragraph
items.notes: Count varies by source: Tao says 25; Economist/X posts say 24; Wikipedia says 28; mathandai.org lists 27 Fields Medalist signatories as of 2026-10-04.

items.headline: The Age of Wonders and Terrors
items.dek: ...we’ll see major math problems getting solved by AIs—even the Clay Millennium Problems. That will be the time to panic! Wake me up when that happens! ... update on the fact that the wild prophecies have come true.
items.author: Scott Aaronson
items.caption: Title + opening: the 2006 skeptic's take, and "the wild prophecies have come true"

items.dek: It seems to me that the Singularity has already started; it’s just wildly unevenly distributed. ... I don’t expect that I’ll ever again prove a theorem because I’m actually needed to prove it.
items.author: Scott Aaronson
items.caption: Paragraph screenshot

items.dek: ...it seems safe to say that human mathematicians are forevermore dethroned as the main theorem-proving entities on planet earth.
items.author: Scott Aaronson
items.caption: Paragraph screenshot

items.dek: By any accounting that doesn’t stack the deck, Eliezer Yudkowsky was right about what the greatest challenge facing civilization in our lifetimes was going to be, and you and I were wrong about it.
items.author: Scott Aaronson
items.caption: Paragraph screenshot (from main post; also quoted in comments)

items.dek: ...today you’re no longer being asked to believe in arguments and extrapolations, but only in the front-page news. Accepting the reality of the coming machine god after it’s solved Navier-Stokes ... is sort of like accepting Jesus after he’s returned to earth on the gleaming cloud.
items.author: Scott Aaronson
items.caption: Paragraph screenshot
items.notes: Same post: his 13-year-old daughter joked "if she wants to become a mathematician, it now looks like she has maybe two more weeks."

items.headline: To grieve, or not to grieve?
items.dek: Language models are solving hard problems which humans could not, and mathematicians are reacting very differently to this news.
items.author: Kevin Buzzard
items.caption: Title + opening paragraph
items.notes: Outline called it "Should we grieve?"; actual title is "To grieve, or not to grieve?". Buzzard frames colleagues' reactions via Kübler-Ross stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression).

items.dek: A faculty member I know who works in fluids told me that the Navier–Stokes news was “extremely depressing”. A post-doc I know told me that they were considering leaving mathematical research because of what it was about to become. A PhD student I know told me that they were stuck on a lemma in their research and ChatGPT one-shotted it and it made them wonder what the point of it all was.
items.author: Kevin Buzzard
items.caption: "Depression" stage paragraph
items.notes: Also: "where exactly do we retreat to when in 1 year’s time AI is not only proving theorems, but also doing a perfectly good job of explaining them to humans?"

items.headline: FLT: Anthropic has beaten me to it
items.dek: ...one of their internal models, using the prove2.me platform, has formalized a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem (FLT) in Lean. This is the final theorem to be formalized in Freek Wiedijk’s famous list of 100 formalization challenges and thus wraps up this 20-year-old benchmark.
items.author: Kevin Buzzard
items.caption: Title + opening paragraph

items.dek: I was given £1M to run my project over 5 years; Anthropic took only 11 days but I do wonder if they spent more money…
items.author: Kevin Buzzard

items.dek: It is a gigantic proof (over 13.4 million lines of code) and takes nearly 20 times as long to compile as Lean’s mathematics library (on a machine with 96 cores!).

facts.claim: OpenAI says 10,000+ AI agents solved the 90-year-old Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem (forced case) in 88 hours, sending 2.7 million messages and producing a 166-page proof plus a Lean formalization.
facts.source: Wikipedia, Navier–Stokes priority controversy; The Guardian; BBC

facts.claim: OpenAI burned at least ~$15 million in compute on the Navier–Stokes proof, which "probably hasn’t yet been read and understood by any human."
facts.source: Scott Aaronson, Shtetl-Optimized

facts.claim: OpenAI: "To solve the Navier–Stokes problem, we used an internal model that is significantly more capable than GPT‑6 Astra."
facts.source: OpenAI announcement (page text)

facts.claim: The unforced Navier–Stokes problem (no external force) is still open; the Clay Institute calls the problem "apparently settled" but verification is "deliberately unhurried."
facts.source: Clay Mathematics Institute; Aaronson; Tapio Schneider guest post on Tao's blog

facts.claim: An Anthropic internal model formalized a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean in 11 days — over 13.4 million lines of code — finishing the last item on the 20-year-old "100 theorems" formalization list. Buzzard had £1M and 5 years for the same goal.
facts.source: Kevin Buzzard, Xena blog

facts.claim: ChatGPT disproved Erdős’ Unit Distance conjecture (May 20, 2026); Claude Fable 5 disproved the Jacobian conjecture (July 2026).
facts.source: Buzzard, Xena blog; VibeMathed dataset; Aaronson

facts.claim: VibeMathed tracks 755 math problems solved with AI (514 fully resolved, 159 Lean-verified), open a combined 11,425 years before AI closed them; ~490 of the tracked entries dated July-September 2026 alone.
facts.source: VibeMathed

facts.claim: arXiv, facing an exponential growth of submissions, now limits each submitter to at most two submissions a month.
facts.source: Terence Tao blog, "arXiv updates its rate limiting policy"

facts.claim: 25+ Fields Medalists signed "A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics": "The goals of the AI companies and the goals of the mathematical community are severely misaligned."
facts.source: mathandai.org; Terence Tao (Mathstodon)

facts.claim: 771 mathematicians' open letter pushed OpenAI to withdraw its sponsorship of Caltech's AI "Mathathon", calling it "slop mathematics."
facts.source: The Next Web; Proofs and Prompts

facts.claim: FrontierMath Tier 4 (research-level problems written by top mathematicians): from 0% (Jan 2025) to 100% (GPT-6.1 Sol, Sep 29 2026).
facts.source: Epoch AI Benchmarking Hub data

facts.claim: Humanity's Last Exam — billed as the last academic exam of its kind — went from 4.6% (Sep 2024 model) to 54.8% (GPT-6 Astra); organizers already ship HLE-Rolling for when models 'hit the noise ceiling.'
facts.source: Epoch AI data; Scale AI/CAIS leaderboard

facts.claim: ARC-AGI-3 launched March 25, 2026 with every frontier model below 1%; six months later GPT-6 Astra scores 62.7% (standard harness) and 99.9% with the provider-adapter harness.
facts.source: ARC Prize leaderboard

facts.claim: The length of software tasks AI agents can finish (50% success) has doubled roughly every 4 months (129 days) since 2023 — from ~4 minutes (GPT-4, 2023) to ~17 hours (Claude Mythos Preview, Apr 2026).
facts.source: METR Time Horizon 1.1 data

facts.claim: GPQA Diamond (PhD-level science questions) went from 35.7% (GPT-4, 2023) to 95.8% (GPT-6 Astra, 2026).
facts.source: Epoch AI data

facts.claim: Strogatz: "I think the year 2026 is going to be remembered as either an annus mirabilis or annus horribilis for mathematics."
facts.source: WIRED

facts.claim: GPT-6 Astra released Sep 3-4 2026; OpenAI president Greg Brockman said it could mark the arrival of AGI. GPT-6 Sol and Luna followed Sep 22, GPT-6.1 Sol Sep 29.
facts.source: Wikipedia GPT-6; NBC; ARC Prize leaderboard

facts.claim: Claude Opus 5.5 (released Sep 22, 2026) scores 64.4% on Humanity's Last Exam without tools and 67.7% with tools (web search, fetch, code execution), per Anthropic's system card — vendor-run, max effort, averaged over five trials.
facts.source: Anthropic, Claude Opus 5.5 System Card, Table 8.1.A and §8.11.1

facts.claim: On Anthropic's own with-tools HLE table: Opus 5.5 67.7%, Claude Fable 5.1 65.6%, Claude Opus 5 63.6%, GPT-6 Astra 57.2%.
facts.source: Anthropic, Introducing Claude Opus 5.5

facts.claim: Independently, Artificial Analysis scores Claude Opus 5.5 at 61.4% on HLE's 2,158 text-only questions — the top score on its leaderboard (previous best 59.1%, Claude Fable 5.1); Gemini 4 Argon 57.1%, GPT-6 Astra 54.7%.
facts.source: Artificial Analysis HLE leaderboard and 'Claude Opus 5.5 takes the top spot' (Sep 22, 2026)

facts.claim: As of Oct 4, 2026 the official Scale AI/CAIS HLE leaderboard (and Epoch AI's HLE data) still does not list Claude Opus 5.5; its top entry remains GPT 6 Astra at 54.80 ±1.94.
facts.source: labs.scale.com HLE leaderboard; Epoch AI benchmark_data.zip hle_external.csv

facts.claim: Q4 2026 so far (Oct 1-4): no new frontier model; the only new model with an HLE score found is InclusionAI's open-weights Ling 3.1 Flash (Oct 1) at 39.4% on Artificial Analysis — so the best score to date is unchanged from Q3.
facts.source: Artificial Analysis model page; Tech Times AI timeline; Digital Applied October 2026 tracker
